Where You Are: The Legal Step, Five of Nine, and What Comes After It

The nine steps of the Medicaid Planning Roadmap, with yours marked.

Download PDF

When a family starts planning ahead, the legal papers can look like the whole job. They're one step of nine, and it's a step you can take at Dad's pace.

This page shows the whole road, where you are on it, and what comes next.

Phase 1 · Assess

Understand where you are today.

  1. 1

    Understand Care Needs → Levels of Care & Costs → Care Plan

    You finish with: Future Care Planning Assessment

  2. 2

    Organize Income & Assets → Ownership & Expenses → Financial File

    You finish with: Family Financial Inventory

  3. 3

    Assess Care & Nonfinancial Eligibility → Income & Assets → Barriers & Readiness

    You finish with: Medicaid Readiness Assessment

Phase 2 · Plan

Develop and implement your strategy.

  1. 4

    Plan Barriers & Issues → Priorities & Professional Team → Written Plan

    You finish with: Advance Medicaid Planning Roadmap

  2. 5

    Legal Authority & Documents → Property, Trusts & Transfers → Attorney Review

    You finish with: Legal Planning Review

    You are here. This step is about Dad's legal papers: which ones exist, where they are, who they name, and which questions belong to an elder law attorney. It's finished when his decision-making and estate-planning documents have been located and reviewed, with an elder law attorney where legal advice is required, and the known Medicaid-related legal issues have been identified for attorney review.

  3. 6

    Financial Costs & Runway → Asset Treatment & Tools → Strategy & Documentation

    You finish with: Long-Term Care Funding Plan

Phase 3 · Secure

Secure benefits, protect assets, and maintain eligibility.

  1. 7

    Apply Prepare → Submit → Manage

    You finish with: Medicaid Application-Ready File

  2. 8

    Protect What May Be Protected → What May Remain Exposed → What Needs Ongoing Attention

    You finish with: Asset Protection Assessment

  3. 9

    Maintain Ongoing Requirements → Changes & Renewals → Maintenance System

    You finish with: Medicaid Monitoring & Maintenance System

What this step produces

A Legal Planning Review: the documents that exist, who they name to make decisions, the ones that are missing or may need another look, your legal questions, and the items for an attorney to review. The family's part of it is a list and a set of questions. It isn't a legal opinion, and completing it doesn't establish that any document is valid, sufficient or current.

What happens next

The legal questions go to an elder law attorney, who advises on powers of attorney, health care documents, wills, trusts and property ownership, and updates documents where needed. The Family Caregiver Alliance says a family can ask the local Area Agency on Aging for a legal consult or hire an attorney who specializes in elder care law.1

After this comes step six, Financial: the financial pieces of the plan, worked through with a licensed financial professional. What you gathered here goes with you. The third phase follows, with Apply, Protect and Maintain. For a family planning ahead, those steps may be a long way off.

This step also comes round again. Your Medicaid planner and the family review the legal plan periodically and after major life events. AARP's legal checklist for family caregivers makes a similar suggestion about a will: review it every few years or during major life changes.2

Who is involved, by role

  • You and your family: finding the papers, writing down what they say, keeping the list of questions.
  • Dad: his wishes, his papers and his decisions. He takes part in all of it.
  • Your Medicaid planner: helps the family inventory the existing documents and identify known Medicaid-related legal issues for attorney review, and reviews the legal plan with the family over time.
  • An elder law attorney: legal advice and legal documents. Advises on powers of attorney, health care documents, wills, trusts and property ownership, and updates documents where needed.

What this page doesn't promise

How long any step takes, who will be available, or how things turn out. Families move through the steps at different speeds, and rules vary by state. Nothing on this page is legal, financial or tax advice.
